---
title: "Login Node Manners"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
- **Goal:** you will keep heavy work and sprawling searches off the shared login node and shared storage, and hand heavy work to the scheduler.
- **Before you start:** [Grow the Carapace](../crypt/rules-of-the-carapace.html). A *login node* is the shared machine you log in to. *Compute nodes* run your jobs. The *scheduler* (here Slurm) decides which job runs where.
- **Time:** about 15 minutes.
:::

Ask your cluster staff before running an agent on the login node. Some sites forbid agents on login nodes altogether, so follow your cluster's user guide where it differs from this page. This quest is read-only, so read it on your laptop.

## Login node versus compute node

Everyone who logs in shares the login node. The scheduler places your jobs on compute nodes. Light work (editing text, `git`, listing one directory, checking a log with `head` or `tail`) is normally fine on the login node. Heavy work belongs on compute nodes: aligners, long foreground pipelines, compressing or indexing big files, building large environments, or running a test suite at scale.

An agent does not know which node it is on or what your site tolerates. It will run a long command if you let it, so you set the rule. It also misjudges "this will only take a few seconds", so tell it to ask when a command's cost is unclear.

Some sites allow agents only inside an interactive compute allocation, and some run a different scheduler with its own commands. If a scheduler command is missing, ask staff and skip near-matches.

## Shared storage prefers scoped searches

Network filesystems can slow down for everyone when something touches huge numbers of files. Agents explore by searching, so a careless `find /` or a recursive `grep -r` from your home or project root is the classic mistake. Ask for searches scoped to one known directory, and keep them away from `/`. The same goes for `du`, `ls --recursive`, `ls --format=long` (it stats every file) and wide globs on big directories, and avoid making many small files in one directory. Keep the agent to your own project paths: other users' or other projects' paths are off limits unless you named them or the site documents them as shared (reference data).

Claude Code's search tools (Glob, Grep) are not a filesystem-load control; scope the search yourself.

## The scheduler's four commands

Four commands cover most of it:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `sbatch` | submit a job script; returns a job ID |
| `srun` | run a job or job step in real time |
| `squeue` | report the state of jobs |
| `scancel` | cancel a pending or running job |

`sbatch --test-only` validates a script and estimates a start time. No job is submitted, so it works as a dry run. Slurm's default time limit is the partition's default, so set limits in the script.

Set `--time`, `--mem` and `--cpus-per-task`, and use a job array for many similar tasks. Write options in their long form (`--dry-run` for `-n`) so you can read what the agent proposes.

Slurm bills by what you allocate, whatever you use. A memory request can also change the CPU count Slurm allocates, because partitions limit memory per CPU (`MaxMemPerCPU`). Above that limit Slurm may raise `--cpus-per-task` to fit the request, or reject the job. Ask your site docs how to read the partition limits. Afterwards compare request, allocation and use with `sacct --jobs=<id> --format=JobID,State,ReqMem,AllocCPUS,MaxRSS`. A job killed for memory shows `OUT_OF_MEMORY` in `State`. `MaxRSS` then understates the need, so raise the request above the failed one.

Scratch space holds throwaway files. Ask where the project's scratch is and use it instead of `/tmp`, which is shared on a login node and often small. A set `$TMPDIR` does not prove you are on scratch, because Slurm can set it to `/tmp`. Scripts, logs and final outputs stay in the project directory.

Before a copy or a delete, find out what it touches. Run `rsync --dry-run --itemize-changes` first, with the same arguments, and read the list. `cp`, `scp` and `rm` have no dry run, so list the exact path or glob and delete only those names. Send large transfers through the scheduler or the site's data-transfer node.

## What the agent's sandbox covers

- Claude Code's sandbox covers shell commands only. File tools, MCP servers and hooks run outside it.
- It fails open by default: if it cannot start, commands run **without** sandboxing, unless `sandbox.failIfUnavailable` is `true`.
- On Linux it needs `bubblewrap` and `socat`. You usually cannot install packages system-wide on a cluster, so ask staff whether they are installed.
- Check that the sandbox is on before you rely on it.

::: {.panel-tabset group="companion"}

## Claude Code

Tell the agent where it may run what, in your project instructions or the prompt, and back it with a permission rule where you can. Useful instructions:

- "Search only inside `./workflow/`. Never run `find` or `grep -r` from `/` or `$HOME`."
- "Run nothing in the foreground on the login node. Draft an `sbatch` script and show it to me."

Instructions are guidance, and the agent can still slip. If a project instruction file (`AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`) is stricter than these lines, the stricter one wins.

Foreground commands time out (default 2 minutes, maximum 10 by default), so a long-running foreground command in the agent's shell is cut off anyway.

## OpenCode + Ollama

The same habits apply. OpenCode's permission model uses allow, ask and deny rules, and an unmatched action asks. Its base policy begins with an allow-all rule, so `sbatch` runs without a prompt until you add a rule. Add explicit rules for the cluster commands, and check your installed version's permission docs. A local model through Ollama runs on the node you are on and touches the filesystem the same way.

:::

- [Configure permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it shows allow, ask and deny rules by command pattern, the way to make heavy or sprawling commands ask first, and warns Bash rules are not a security boundary.
- [sbatch](https://slurm.schedmd.com/sbatch.html): SchedMD (Slurm), docs. Why read: it is the manual for submitting jobs, including --test-only to validate a request without submitting.
